Context: Imagine that you have time-traveled back to the year 1894. It is one year before the Lumiere Brothers will show a moving picture to an audience for the first time. But you have the luxury of taking one movie back with you to show to an audience. Which film do you take with you to show them?

Ground Rules: it must be a theatrically released film. No TV shows, mini-series, web-series, episodes, webisodes, mobisodes, viral videos, home movies, etc. Short films are fair game if they were shown in a theater. Any film you pick will transfer the technology of its exhibition. If it is in color, it stays in color. If it is 3D, it stays 3D, etc. For the sake of argument, let us imagine that the audience that will be viewing this film will be randomly sampled, so there is no way to account for any demographic, including sex, age, race, religion, geographical location, etc.

Consider the Following: Do you select a film that is tried-and-true, and time-tested already? Or do you select something with state-of-the-art visuals and cutting-edge technology? Do you select an adaptation of a pre-1894 story that they may be familiar with or select something modern and/or original? What is of importance when deciding the first motion picture that an audience could see?

The Host's Response: After much consideration, my official selection is Mary Poppins. There were two priorities for me when making a selection: first, I do not want to blow their mind too much, and second, I wanted to make sure it had broad appeal. By selecting a film that is appropriate for the entire family, I will not have to worry about demographics, and because the film is set in 1910, the audience is more likely to understand the plot of the film, as it takes place in the near future. It also utilizes music a great deal, and with both Dick Van Dyke and Julie Andrews as its stars, which will also contribute to its broad appeal. Additionally, the film is far enough along in terms of cinematic technology that its visual effects are amazing. It is a time-tested film, and I think this would be the perfect selection for an audience that had never seen a film before.
Q: Which film would you show to a pre-movie audience?
